title: Units and Measurements
prerequisites: Familiarity with metre, kilogram and second.
Ability to work with powers of ten.
Basic idea of area and volume.
Knowledge that every measurement carries some uncertainty.

topics.title: Physical Quantities and the SI System
topics.quick_summary: Physical quantities are measured against agreed standards, and the SI system defines seven base units from which all other units are derived.
topics.real_life: The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one team used pounds and another newtons — a $125 million reminder that units are not a formality.

detailed.definition: A physical quantity is anything that can be measured. A unit is the agreed standard against which it is measured. Base units are independent and cannot be derived from one another; derived units are combinations of base units.
detailed.key_idea: There are exactly seven SI base units. Every other unit in physics — newton, joule, watt, pascal — is built from these seven by multiplication and division alone.
detailed.working_principle: A measurement is meaningless without a unit, and the numerical value is inversely proportional to the size of the unit chosen. The same length is 1 m or 100 cm — a larger unit gives a smaller number.
applications: Newton (N) = kg·m/s²; Joule (J) = kg·m²/s²; Watt (W) = kg·m²/s³.
Prefixes: kilo (10³), mega (10⁶), giga (10⁹), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶), nano (10⁻⁹).
Astronomical unit and light year are convenient units for very large distances.

points: Seven SI base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), candela (luminous intensity).
Derived units are combinations of base units; e.g. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².
Unit symbols named after scientists are capitalised (N, J, W, K) but written in full in lower case (newton, joule).
Never write a plural 's' on a unit symbol — 5 kg, not 5 kgs.
1 light year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m — a unit of distance, not of time.
mistakes: Calling the light year a unit of time; it is a unit of distance.
Writing 'Kg' or 'KG' instead of 'kg' — only the prefix rules decide capitalisation.
Treating the newton as a base unit; it is derived.
topics.memory_hook: 'Metre, Kilogram, Second, Ampere, Kelvin, Mole, Candela' — 'My King Sends A Knight, Mounted, Charging.'
topics.advanced: Since 2019 every SI base unit is defined by fixing a fundamental constant — the kilogram through Planck's constant, the metre through the speed of light. No physical artefact remains, so the units cannot drift over time.

topics.title: Measuring Instruments — Vernier Callipers and Screw Gauge
topics.quick_summary: A vernier calliper measures to 0.1 mm and a screw gauge to 0.01 mm, using a scale that magnifies a fraction of the smallest main-scale division.
topics.real_life: A mechanic checks the diameter of a piston with a screw gauge because a metre rule simply cannot resolve the hundredth of a millimetre that decides whether an engine seizes.

detailed.definition: Least count is the smallest measurement that an instrument can read accurately. For a vernier calliper it is the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier-scale division.
detailed.key_idea: Both instruments work by the same trick: a second scale is made slightly different from the first, so the point at which two divisions coincide reveals a fraction of the smallest main-scale division.
detailed.working_principle: Total reading = main scale reading + (vernier or circular scale coincidence × least count). Zero error must be found first and subtracted algebraically from every reading.
applications: Vernier calliper: internal and external diameters, depths of hollow cylinders.
Screw gauge: thickness of a wire, a sheet of paper or a glass slide.
Both are used in workshops, laboratories and quality control.

points: Least count of vernier calliper = 1 MSD − 1 VSD, usually 0.1 mm or 0.01 cm.
Least count of screw gauge = pitch / number of circular scale divisions, usually 0.01 mm.
Pitch = distance moved on the main scale in one complete rotation of the screw.
Total reading = MSR + (coincidence × LC), then correct for zero error.
Positive zero error is subtracted; negative zero error is added.
mistakes: Adding a positive zero error instead of subtracting it.
Using the number of vernier divisions instead of the coincidence number in the formula.
Forgetting to convert the final reading into the required unit.
topics.memory_hook: 'Correct reading = Observed reading − Zero error' — sign and all, every single time.
topics.advanced: The vernier principle dates to 1631 and remains in use because it needs no power and cannot drift. Digital callipers replace the eye with a capacitive encoder but rely on exactly the same geometrical idea.

formulas.name: Least Count of a Vernier Calliper
formulas.variables: MSD = one main scale division, VSD = one vernier scale division.
formulas.when_to_use: Before taking any reading with a vernier calliper.
formulas.shortcut: LC also equals (value of 1 MSD) ÷ (number of vernier divisions).

formulas.name: Least Count of a Screw Gauge
formulas.formula: LC = Pitch / Number of circular scale divisions
formulas.variables: Pitch = distance advanced in one full rotation, usually 0.5 mm or 1 mm.
formulas.when_to_use: Before taking any reading with a screw gauge or micrometer.
formulas.common_mistakes: Using the total number of main scale divisions instead of circular scale divisions.
formulas.shortcut: Pitch 1 mm with 100 divisions gives the standard LC of 0.01 mm.

topics.title: Errors and Significant Figures
topics.quick_summary: Every measurement carries an error; significant figures record how precisely a quantity is known, and a calculated result can never be more precise than the least precise measurement used.
topics.real_life: Reporting a body's mass as 52.3846 kg after weighing it on a bathroom scale claims a precision the instrument never had.

detailed.definition: Systematic errors have a definite cause and always shift readings in the same direction; random errors vary unpredictably. Significant figures are the digits in a measurement that are known reliably plus one uncertain digit.
detailed.key_idea: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another. A measurement can be precise but inaccurate — for example, a scale with a zero error.
detailed.working_principle: Random errors are reduced by taking the mean of many readings. Systematic errors are not — they must be removed by correcting the instrument, which is why zero error is checked before measuring.
applications: In addition and subtraction, the result keeps as many decimal places as the least precise term.
In multiplication and division, the result keeps as many significant figures as the least precise factor.
Zero error in callipers and screw gauges is a classic systematic error.

points: All non-zero digits are significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant.
Leading zeros are not significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point are.
Accuracy = closeness to the true value; Precision = repeatability.
Random errors are reduced by averaging; systematic errors are not.
The final answer must not have more significant figures than the least precise input.
mistakes: Quoting a calculator result to eight digits when the data justify only three.
Counting leading zeros in 0.0025 as significant — there are only two significant figures.
Assuming averaging removes all errors; it only reduces random ones.
topics.memory_hook: 'Accurate = on target; Precise = tightly grouped' — you can be one without the other.
topics.advanced: Errors propagate predictably: for a product or quotient, the fractional errors add. So if a radius is known to 1%, the volume of a sphere is known only to 3%, because the radius is cubed.
